title: Preparing your hoop for cross-stitch
subtitle: How to mount fabric taut without distorting the weave
excerpt: A cross-stitch hoop holds the Aida fabric taut while you stitch, which keeps tension even and makes the holes easy to see. The fabric must be mounted taut but not so tight it distorts the weave. Take the hoop off the fabric between sessions to avoid hoop marks.
sourceNotes: Hoop preparation methods documented in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Standard practice for wooden round hoops is unchanged since the Victorian era.

glossaryTerms.definition: Two concentric rings, usually of wood or plastic, that hold fabric taut for embroidery or cross-stitch. The inner ring is placed under the fabric; the outer ring has a screw tensioner and clamps over the top. Tightening the screw pulls the fabric firm between the two rings.

lie flat. The standard round hoop for cross-stitch is six inches in diameter. Pick a hoop that is at least two inches wider than the longest edge of your design.
Turn the screw counterclockwise until the outer ring separates easily from the inner ring. Do not force it.
Place the inner ring under the fabric.
Lay the fabric over the inner ring with the design area centred. The right side of the fabric faces upward.
Press the outer ring down over the inner ring.
Push the outer ring down over the fabric and inner ring. The fabric is now sandwiched between the two rings.
Pull the fabric edges taut and tighten the screw.

Hold the fabric at the edges and pull gently outward from opposite sides. The fabric should feel drum-tight without the weave distorting. Tighten the screw to hold the tension. The Aida grid should remain perfectly square inside the hoop.

Wooden hoops can leave a ring-shaped mark on the fabric if they stay in place for more than a few hours. Remove the hoop from the fabric after each stitching session. The mark usually washes out, but on fine or vintage Aida it can be permanent. Tissue paper wrapped around the inner ring before mounting reduces the pressure and helps prevent marks.

A hoop that is too small forces you to reposition it repeatedly, which puts stress on the stitches. A hoop that is too large is unwieldy to hold and grip. For small motifs of five to eight centimetres, a four-inch or five-inch hoop is comfortable. For medium designs of ten to fifteen centimetres, a six-inch or seven-inch hoop. For large samplers, a ten-inch or twelve-inch hoop, or a scroll frame rather than a round hoop.
